title: Observe Correct Handling and Dispatch of Chilled Carcasses

lessons.title: Chilling and checking carcasses before dispatch
lessons.html:
Why chilling matters

Bacteria grow quickly on warm meat. After inspection and washing, carcasses go into the chiller so that the deep muscle temperature drops quickly. Proper chilling slows bacteria, keeps meat safe and gives it a longer shelf life. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations require meat to be kept at safe temperatures, and the abattoir's procedures set the temperature that carcasses must reach before they may leave.

Good chiller practice

  • Carcasses hang without touching each other or the walls and floor, so cold air can move around them.
  • The chiller is not overloaded. Too many warm carcasses at once raise the room temperature.
  • Doors stay closed as much as possible.
  • Passed meat is kept apart from detained or condemned meat at all times.
  • The chiller temperature is recorded at set times on a chart or electronic logger.

Checks before dispatch

As the meat examiner you observe that dispatch follows the rules. Before carcasses are loaded:

  1. Check that each carcass carries the approved inspection mark and, where it applies, the classification marks.
  2. Check that the deep muscle temperature, measured with a clean, calibrated probe thermometer in the thickest part (such as the hindquarter), meets the limit in the abattoir's procedure.
  3. Look for contamination that happened in the chiller: dirt, dripping condensation, contact with the floor, or mould.
  4. Check that detained carcasses are not loaded until the veterinarian has released them.

Sterilise the probe between carcasses so you do not spread bacteria into the deep muscle.

lessons.title: Loading, transport and records
lessons.html:
Loading hygiene

The cold chain can be broken at the loading bay. Watch the loading process closely.

  • The loading area should be enclosed or covered, with a dock seal or curtain, so meat is not exposed to dust, rain, flies or heat.
  • Carcasses should move on rails directly into the vehicle. If they must be carried, workers wear clean protective clothing and head covers, and the meat must never touch the ground.
  • Workers who handle meat must not also handle hides, offal waste or condemned material without changing and washing.

The vehicle

Inspect the truck before loading:

  • It is refrigerated and pre-cooled to the required temperature.
  • The inside is clean, with no smell, old blood or meat scraps.
  • Carcasses hang on rails and do not lie on the floor.
  • Meat is not transported with chemicals, animals or other goods that could contaminate it.

If a vehicle is dirty or not cold, tell the dispatch supervisor that it may not be loaded until the problem is corrected.

Records

Dispatch records show where every carcass went. They usually include the date, carcass numbers, number of carcasses, temperatures, vehicle registration and the customer. These records make it possible to trace and recall meat if a problem is found later.

What never to do

  • Never dispatch a carcass without the inspection mark.
  • Never dispatch warm meat to save time.
  • Never pick up a carcass that has fallen on the floor and load it; it must be trimmed or handled according to procedure.

Key points

  • Carcasses must be chilled to the temperature in the abattoir's procedure before dispatch.
  • Measure deep muscle temperature with a clean, calibrated probe.
  • Check for the inspection mark on every carcass.
  • Inspect the vehicle: clean, refrigerated and pre-cooled.
  • Keep dispatch records so meat can be traced and recalled.
